pool.q: In a large language model, what is a token?
options: A password for the model's API
A chunk of text made of a variable number of characters
pool.explain: The tokenizer splits input into tokens, and each token is mapped to an integer index.
pool.evidence: A token is a chunk of text – consisting of a variable number of characters, so the tokenizer's main task is splitting the input into an array of tokens.

pool.q: How does a large language model produce its next token?
options: It predicts a probability distribution over possible next tokens
It copies the next word from its training data
It picks a random dictionary word
It always chooses the shortest word
pool.explain: The distribution comes from what the model learned in training.
pool.evidence: This is because the model predicts a probability distribution over all possible ‘next tokens’, calculated based on its training.

pool.q: Is the most probable token always the one chosen?
pool.explain: Some randomness makes output more varied and creative.
pool.evidence: However, not always is the token with the highest probability chosen from the resulting distribution.

pool.q: What is an embedding?
options: A video embedded in a web page
A model that writes long essays
A numerical representation of the input text
A summary written by a human
pool.explain: Embeddings turn text into numbers so similar meanings end up close together.
pool.evidence: Embeddings are a set of models that can convert text into a numerical form, called embedding, which is a numerical representation of the input text.

pool.q: Why can an AI service's name differ from the underlying model's name?
options: Model names are kept secret by law
Every request uses a brand-new model
Services often route requests between several model variants
Service names are chosen at random
pool.explain: Check which model actually answers when comparing options.
pool.evidence: Modern AI services often route between several model variants, so the service name and the underlying model name are not always the same thing.

pool.q: What are embedding models often used for?
options: Transfer learning, reusing weights learned on a data-rich task
pool.explain: The learned embeddings are reused for other downstream tasks.
pool.evidence: Embedding models are often used for transfer learning

pool.q: What are text generation models typically trained on?
options: Large text datasets, such as BookCorpus
pool.explain: They can then generate new text or answer questions.
pool.evidence: Text generation models are often trained on large datasets of text, such as BookCorpus

pool.q: Which tasks are LLMs good at, according to the lesson?
options: Exact arithmetic on very large numbers
Summarising text, extracting insights and producing text such as CVs
pool.explain: Text generation apps build on these strengths.
pool.evidence: LLMs are great at things like summarizing text, getting insights from text, producing text like resumes and more.

pool.q: How do you change how random or creative a model's output is?
pool.explain: Higher temperature gives more varied output; lower gives more predictable output.
pool.evidence: To alter the temperature, you can use the temperature parameter.

pool.q: What should you consider about tokens when building a text generation app?
options: How many tokens you need to generate the text you want
Only the colour of the tokens
pool.explain: Token limits cap the length of the response and affect cost.
pool.evidence: We should consider how many tokens we need to generate the text we want.

pool.q: What usually controls access to an SDK's or API's services?
options: A unique key or authentication token
pool.explain: Keys must be kept secret, never committed to code.
pool.evidence: which is often through the use of a unique key or authentication token

pool.q: Why do SDKs and APIs make maintenance easier?
options: They remove the need for testing
They write your code for you
Updates often just mean updating a library
pool.explain: New versions bring improvements without rewriting your app.
pool.evidence: Updates and improvements are easier to manage as most APIs and SDKs simply require an update to a library when a newer version is released.

pool.q: After deploying a chat app, what should you monitor besides functionality?
options: The number of colours in the UI
How well it follows the six principles of responsible AI
pool.explain: Quality includes fairness, reliability, safety and more.
pool.evidence: both in terms of functionality and adhering to the six principles of responsible AI

pool.q: What can embeddings (vectors) be used for in a search application?
pool.explain: Searching by meaning compares the vectors of the query and the documents.
pool.evidence: Embeddings are numerical representations of data also known as vectors, and can be used for semantic search for data.

pool.q: What problem did LLM responses have before function calling?
options: They could only be in English
They were too slow to use
pool.explain: Function calling returns structured output your code can rely on.
pool.evidence: Before function calling, responses from an LLM were unstructured and inconsistent.

pool.q: What should you remember about function definitions sent to the model?
options: They go into the system message and use up available tokens
They are hidden from the model
pool.explain: Large or many function definitions reduce space for the conversation.
pool.evidence: Functions are included in the system message to the LLM and will be included in the amount of available tokens you have available.

pool.q: How do applications use the structured responses from function calling?
options: To decide which function to run
pool.explain: For example, sending an email or querying a database.
pool.evidence: We then use those structured responses to know what function to run in our applications.

pool.q: Which two ways does the lesson give for putting trust at the centre of AI app design?
pool.explain: Users trust a system they can understand and steer.
pool.evidence: Two ways to ensure that trust is put right at the center of design are explainability and control.

pool.q: In retrieval augmented generation (RAG), what is the retriever's job?
options: To retrain the model every night
To get documents that provide context and ground the LLM on your data
To translate answers into other languages
pool.explain: Retrieved passages are added to the prompt so answers are based on your own data.
pool.evidence: The goal of the retriever is to get documents that will be used to provide context and ground the LLM on your data.

pool.q: Why can't a standard LLM chatbot answer from a company's internal product manual?
options: Confidential information like internal manuals is not in its training data
pool.explain: RAG retrieves such documents and adds them to the prompt.
pool.evidence: the data used to train LLMs excludes confidential information such as personal notes or a company's product manual

pool.q: Without retrieval, what limits an LLM chatbot's responses?
options: The context provided and its foundational training data
pool.explain: Its knowledge also stops at its training cutoff.
pool.evidence: However, its responses are limited to the context provided and its foundational training data.

pool.q: For a model to meet the traditional definition of open source, which information should be publicly available?
options: The datasets used to train the model, among other things
pool.explain: Openness also covers weights, training code and licence terms.
pool.evidence: For a model to be aligned with the traditional definition of open source the following information should be publicly available: Datasets used to train the model.

pool.q: In this course, what does fine-tuning refer to?
options: Supervised fine-tuning: retraining the model with new data that was not in its original training set
Running the same model on a faster GPU
pool.explain: Fine-tuning changes the model's weights; prompting and RAG do not.
pool.evidence: we are referring to supervised fine-tuning where the retraining is done by adding new data that was not part of the original training dataset.

pool.q: What is one limitation of few-shot learning?
options: Token limits restrict how many examples you can give
It needs no examples at all
pool.explain: Fine-tuning can overcome this by training on many examples.
pool.evidence: Model token limits can restrict the number of examples you can give, and limit the effectiveness

pool.q: What are large language models pre-trained on?
options: Large quantities of text from diverse sources, including the internet
pool.explain: Fine-tuning then adapts them to a specific task or domain.
pool.evidence: large language models are pre-trained on large quantities of text sourced from diverse sources including the internet

pool.q: Why are small language models (SLMs) a good fit for some applications?
options: They always know more facts than large models
They do not need any training data
They can only be used offline
They are compact and efficient, ideal where computational resources are limited
pool.explain: SLMs trade breadth for efficiency and can run on modest hardware.
pool.evidence: SLMs are more compact and efficient, making them ideal for applications where computational resources are limited.

pool.q: Why are small language models less susceptible to some biases?
options: They are trained on more constrained, domain-specific data
pool.explain: They are still not immune to bias.
pool.evidence: SLMs, being trained on more constrained, domain-specific datasets, are inherently less susceptible to such biases

pool.q: How are small language models typically built?
options: By training on a single sentence
By compressing or distilling larger models
pool.explain: They aim to keep much of the larger model's capability.
pool.evidence: Typically, SLMs are constructed by compressing or distilling LLMs

pool.q: Where can models like Phi-3.5-mini be deployed, unlike large LLMs?
pool.explain: Small models suit resource-constrained environments.
pool.evidence: Unlike LLM, you can deploy Phi-3/3.5-mini or Phi-3/3.5-Vision on edge devices.

pool.q: What are AI agents, in simple terms?
options: Systems that let LLMs act, by giving them tools and knowledge
pool.explain: Agents can act on the world, not just respond to prompts.
pool.evidence: AI Agents are systems that let Large Language Models (LLMs) actually do things

pool.q: What does 'easily accessible yet occasionally invisible' mean for an agent?
options: It is hidden from all users
It works in the background and only nudges you when relevant
It only works on one device
pool.explain: It stays discoverable for authorised users on any device.
pool.evidence: agent largely operates in the background and only nudges us when it is relevant and appropriate

pool.q: What does the design principle 'connecting, not collapsing' mean?
options: Helping connect people to other people, events and knowledge
Reducing all choices to one option
pool.explain: Agents should enable collaboration and connection.
pool.evidence: help connect people to other people, events, and actionable knowledge to enable collaboration and connection

pool.q: Why are tools important for AI agents?
options: They allow agents to have a broader range of capabilities
They replace the language model entirely
pool.explain: Functions let an agent act — call APIs, query data, run code — beyond generating text.
pool.evidence: Tools are interesting because they allow AI agents to have a broader range of capabilities.

pool.q: Why are 'function' and 'tool' often used interchangeably for agents?
options: Functions are the tools agents use to carry out tasks
They are two names for prompts
pool.explain: Tools give agents a much wider range of actions.
pool.evidence: You will often see 'Function' and 'Tool' used interchangeably because 'functions' (blocks of reusable code) are the 'tools' agents use to carry out tasks.

pool.q: What is the distinguishing quality of an agentic (RAG) system?
options: It answers in a single step
Its ability to own its reasoning process
pool.explain: Agentic RAG evaluates results, refines queries and calls more tools until the answer is good enough.
pool.evidence: The distinguishing quality of an agentic system is its ability to own its reasoning process.

pool.q: How does an agentic RAG system work through a task?
options: It asks the user to search
It evaluates results, refines queries and uses tools until it reaches a good answer
pool.explain: This iterative maker-checker loop improves correctness.
pool.evidence: The system evaluates results, refines queries, invokes additional tools if needed, and continues this cycle until a satisfactory solution is achieved.
